say.text: A classmate writes: 'TOF is a VSD, an overriding aorta, pulmonary stenosis, plus ASD and PDA. More holes, more blue.'
Which correction is best?

choices.label: ASD and PDA may accompany TOF but are not among the four
Keep ASD as the fourth component; PDA is the extra
Swap ASD and PDA for LVH; the left ventricle overworks
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. ASD and PDA are among the other anomalies that may accompany TOF; the four components listed by StatPearls and CDC include no ASD, PDA or LVH.
The four: a large anteriorly malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta, infundibular RVOT obstruction and right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH).

Tempting, because an ASD really does turn up with TOF and the pentalogy name uses it. But a hole that turns up alongside is not a component: the four listed by StatPearls and CDC include no ASD or PDA.
The four are the VSD, overriding aorta, infundibular obstruction and RVH.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note the exam form: PYQs have keyed PDA, ASD and LVH as 'not part of TOF'; current StatPearls lists the four as VSD, overriding aorta, RVOT obstruction and RVH.

say.text: Tempting, because an overriding aorta sounds like left-heart work. But the four components listed by StatPearls and CDC include no LVH.
The thick ventricle in TOF is the right one: RVH, secondary to chronic systemic pressures.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: PYQs have keyed LVH, with ASD and PDA, as 'not part of TOF'.

say.text: Look at the word 'may'. Some lesions merely turn up beside TOF. Which of the classmate's five are defining, and which only accompany?
Second belief: 'TOF is a pulmonary valve disease.'
Where does the RVOT (right ventricular outflow tract) obstruction sit in classic TOF?

choices.label: In the left ventricular outflow tract

say.text: Yes. The obstruction is infundibular (sub-pulmonary) RVOT obstruction, one of the four components.
Tempting, because the pulmonary valve is the name we attach to pulmonary stenosis. But the component is infundibular (sub-pulmonary) RVOT obstruction, below the valve.
Tempting, because the aorta overrides and the left side feels involved. But the obstruction is infundibular (sub-pulmonary) RVOT obstruction, on the right.
Now follow the blood. The VSD is large, the aorta overrides, and the infundibulum is narrowed.
With significant obstruction, where does most of the right ventricular blood go?

choices.label: Across the VSD to the aorta, bypassing the lungs
Into the lungs; flow rises and the film turns plethoric

say.text: Yes. With significant RVOT obstruction, most of the blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.
Tempting, because a VSD usually sends blood to the lungs. But here the outflow is blocked, so most blood shunts toward the aorta and bypasses the pulmonary bed.
The right ventricle now pumps against that block and the systemic pressure. Which ventricle thickens, and how does it fit the chain?

choices.label: Right ventricle; the thick wall is what narrows the outflow
Right ventricle; thickening is secondary to systemic pressures
Left ventricle, since it feeds the overriding aorta
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures, so it comes last in the chain, not first.
Tempting, because a thick wall and a narrow outflow sit side by side. But the arrow runs the other way: RVH is secondary to chronic systemic pressures.
The narrowing is the infundibular obstruction, a separate component.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: RVH is a consequence in this chain, never the cause of the obstruction.

say.text: Tempting, because the aorta overrides. But the component is right ventricular hypertrophy, secondary to chronic systemic pressures; LVH is not one of the four.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one is worth a second look: PYQs have keyed LVH as 'not part of TOF'.

say.text: Ask which side meets the block and the aortic pressure. Is the thickening a cause of the narrowing, or a response to it?
Chain to keep: malaligned VSD, overriding aorta, infundibular obstruction, blood bypasses the lungs, RV pressure up, RVH last.
Last belief: 'Pentalogy of Fallot is TOF plus a PDA, five lesions in all.'
What does the fifth lesion actually add?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Pentalogy of Fallot is TOF plus an atrial septal defect; the term is old and seldom used now.
PYQs have expected the same, and CDC confirms it.
Tempting, because PDA is the other lesion named beside ASD as accompanying TOF. But the pentalogy is TOF plus an atrial septal defect.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note: PYQs have expected pentalogy = TOF + ASD; CDC agrees.

say.text: Tempting, because a VSD is already the core of TOF. But the fifth lesion is an atrial septal defect, not another VSD.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note: PYQs have expected pentalogy = TOF + ASD; CDC agrees.

say.text: Think of the two chambers on top, not the vessels or the ventricles. Which hole sits there?
Core rebuilt. Want the optional side-branch on arch and syndrome numbers?
Quick refutation: someone says a right aortic arch is 'about 6% or up to 15%' in TOF.
What is the right aortic arch figure?
Yes. A right aortic arch is seen in 20-25% of TOF.
Tempting, because those figures sound familiar. They belong to 22q11.2 deletion frequency: up to 15% in some sources, 6% in one cohort.
The right aortic arch is seen in 20-25%.
Which statement about syndromes in TOF is best?

choices.label: Down syndrome is the usual association
22q11.2 deletion is present in most TOF cases
22q11.2 deletion is the commonest link, in a minority

say.text: Yes. 22q11.2 deletion is the most common syndromic association, in up to 15% of cases.
Sources differ: up to 15% versus 6% in one cohort.
Tempting, because Down syndrome is the famous heart-defect syndrome. But the most common syndromic association is the 22q11.2 deletion.
Tempting, because it is the top association. But sources differ on its frequency: up to 15% versus 6% in one cohort, not most cases.
